claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies act as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile loading.
Controlled post-solidification thermal cycling can induce coherent secondary precipitates along lamellar-colony boundaries.
Boundary-localized coherent secondary precipitates will increase tensile strength.
Boundary-localized coherent secondary precipitates will increase room-temperature tensile ductility.
The coherent precipitates blunt stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
The coherent precipitates impede microcrack initiation and propagation.
Thermally induced precipitates strengthen the boundary regions.
The precipitates increase yield strength by acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
The precipitates improve plasticity by promoting localized stress redistribution.
Reduced microcrack-triggered catastrophic failure will enhance ductility relative to conventionally processed lamellar colonies.
Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness because microcracks initiate at internal boundaries.
The intervention is beneficial only when the alloy composition permits stable coherent precipitates to form without altering the overall dual-phase lamellar structure.
The intervention may be ineffective when thermal-cycling parameters are not optimized.
The intervention may be ineffective when the alloy lacks the elements needed to form stable precipitates.
